text:
Search found no direct BERT4Rec study showing activation-patching-guided training outperforms behavioral-history ablations under matched search budgets. Evidence remains indirect: [Zhang and Nanda](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16042) show localization depends strongly on corruption methods and measurement choices in language models; identifying influential components does not establish that modifying them improves recommendation. Meanwhile, [BERT4Rec replication experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07483) found substantial undertraining and implementation effects—original-code replication required up to 30× longer training, while an optimized implementation reduced convergence time by up to 95%. These findings favor checking convergence and basic training choices before expensive localization.

Patching requires clean and corrupted runs plus intervention runs. With cached reference activations, scanning K sites implies roughly K+2 forward passes per diagnostic batch; this is an operation-count estimate, not measured BERT4Rec runtime. No directly comparable diagnostic wall-clock costs or training gains were located. A useful experiment would compare localization-guided changes against recent-history truncation, order shuffling, and item-removal diagnostics, giving each arm the same total GPU budget and one trained BERT4Rec per category. Measure diagnostic time, retraining time, and resulting macro validation HR@10. Practical potential appears plausible but unproven; a high benefit rating is currently unsupported.

Adaptive validation reuse can produce selection bias comparable to differences between algorithms, as [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) demonstrate. For this benchmark, preserve pinned splits, candidates, seeds, and evaluator; predeclare comparison arms and search budgets, record every attempted configuration, and leave held-out testing to the host after selection. Fixed evaluation seeds improve comparability but do not prevent adaptive validation overfitting.
